title: Eden Before Mars
spine: Bring the conditional off-world engineering comparison to an explicitly imagined public path, expose a stopped machine’s dependency on parts and service information, then connect ecological limits and the right to challenge a plan with the book’s proposed constitution of constructive capacity.

source.scope: Full99-section map and complete prior20-line film; complete sources7,8,13,14,24,67,73,79,80 read. This covers the preface, quantitative-method note, constructive utopia, planetary mirror test, writing/memory chapter, capture safeguards, constructive constitution, epilogue and method note. Selected source reading, not the whole210k-character work or external bibliography audit.
source.genre: Comparative technological history and explicitly conditional constructive utopia, with material scenarios and proposed constitutional safeguards.
source.images: Only source image is the cover, inspected: split green Earth-like city and barren orange world with domed shelters/robot. It is a speculative cover composition, not a technical diagram. Original local repair and ecological planning scenes enact its questions without using the cover as evidence.

scenes.title: The question comes home
lines: Eden Before Mars asks why technologies for hostile worlds should change expectations here on Earth.
If autonomous construction matures, ordinary towns could gain new ways to repair and build.
Earth already has air, water, infrastructure, and people with claims to the land.
The book's challenge is to expand local capability without enclosing life behind new gatekeepers.
It joins technological history with an explicitly conditional proposal for a more inhabitable world.
scenes.emotionalPlan: A distant technical ambition turns into a nearby civic possibility, then into a question about people and place.
scenes.artPlan: Begin on an ordinary inhabited square with a broken uneven path, useful mature shade tree, homes and adults discussing its repair. In a small clearly marked conditional comparison, a robotic vehicle beside a simple unoccupied off-world habitat handles local material; do not depict an existing Mars settlement or a launch forecast. Bring focus back to Earth’s existing tree, water supply and neighbors with different uses of the square. A supported dormant construction machine and salvaged stone represent a possible capacity to improve it. Burnt-orange equipment, olive trees, turquoise water, warm limestone and violet civic clothing create an original daylight identity. No completed utopia or uniform grid of garden icons.

scenes.title: A machine can bring dependence
lines: Imagine a town reusing stone for a shaded public path.
A robotic machine might reduce the work of handling irregular materials.
But one failed component can stop the work while the material remains available.
If only one supplier can repair it, the town's freedom depends on that supplier.
The book asks who controls construction after the machine makes building cheaper.
scenes.emotionalPlan: Practical possibility meets a small but consequential interruption, exposing an institutional dependency inside a material tool.
scenes.artPlan: Close into the same explicitly imagined public-path project. Salvaged irregular stones sit in a supported stack beside the existing mature tree and an inactive compact machine. Show a distinct failed component in the machine’s maintenance bay and the corresponding empty spare compartment; never give a live repair procedure. The crew can inspect a general service diagram, but the matching replacement part and service information remain with a single supplier. The crew’s request reaches that supplier without a promised delivery. No floating key, abstract gate or dialogue pretending the issue is solved. Keep the machine clearly stopped, people clear of moving equipment, and the path unfinished. This is a hypothetical illustration of the book’s maintenance-chain and right-to-repair arguments, not a documented equipment failure.

scenes.title: Earth is already alive
lines: Difficulties also remain when the machinery is available and the community agrees.
A proposed water feature still needs a water budget and room for living systems.
More garden-like settlements should reduce pressure on wild places, rather than landscape everything.
The historical chapters explain why technical power has repeatedly supported cooperation and domination.
That history makes repair, oversight, and the freedom to refuse part of the design.
scenes.emotionalPlan: The focus widens from the machine to ecological limits and the inhabitants who can contest a plan.
scenes.artPlan: Change to a landscape planning view around the square and an adjoining living wetland. A proposed ornamental water feature has a visibly finite source, and its footprint initially conflicts with the established vegetation corridor. The discussion narrows the proposed footprint without instantly creating new habitat, water or mature trees. Keep the existing wild area distinct from an intensively tended town garden. At the historical sentence, retain the SAME present imagined town and its water plan. Show the actual allocation/maintenance record belonging to this hypothetical project and a resident asking to inspect it; an official’s sole custody initially limits that scrutiny. This is explicitly the present invented example of the book’s historical pattern, not an old artifact or pseudo-historical episode. No road remains while the visual concerns records. Retain material/ecological limits rather than turning the image into a universal ideal landscape.

scenes.title: The garden needs a constitution
lines: The proposed constitution gives communities capacity to build and obligations to maintain.
Residents need reasons for decisions, alternative providers, and ways to challenge plans.
A repairable machine helps only when the parts, knowledge, and authority are accessible.
Begin with the Planetary Mirror Test, then examine the Constitution of Constructive Capacity.
Read it to ask what a beautiful place must let its inhabitants control.
scenes.emotionalPlan: The constructive release is access to real choices and continuing care, not a machine-made paradise.
scenes.artPlan: Return to the stopped machine as an explicitly proposed local-maintenance arrangement. Two independent service options can inspect the same understandable documentation and compatible spare part. A resident’s concern about the wetland remains beside the project plan and can reach an independent reviewer; neither a provider’s approval nor a majority vote automatically overrides ecological limits. The scene does not perform a hazardous repair, resume the excavator instantly or finish the path. Close on the actual source book opened to the two named sections, with the maintenance obligation and protected living corridor still visible in the background. The promise is capacity plus contestability and care, not a guaranteed technical, legal or environmental outcome.

evidence.heading: Preface: The Garden as a Theory of History
evidence.quote: None of this proves that large extraterrestrial settlements are imminent.

evidence.heading: Preface: The Garden as a Theory of History
evidence.quote: Here we already possess an atmosphere, liquid water, biological productivity, established cities, transport networks, knowledge institutions, and billions of skilled people.

evidence.heading: Preface: The Garden as a Theory of History
evidence.quote: Engineering gets easier; legitimacy gets harder.

evidence.heading: Preface: The Garden as a Theory of History
evidence.quote: A photovoltaic panel has a supply chain; a battery contains refined minerals; an autonomous machine requires maintenance, cybersecurity, spare parts, and institutions capable of saying no.

evidence.heading: The Constructive Utopia
evidence.quote: It proposes that communities gain a constitutional right and a practical capability to shape their local material environment.

evidence.heading: The Constructive Utopia
evidence.quote: Autonomous or semi-autonomous machines could lower the labor cost of handling local stone, earth, timber, recycled components, and vegetation.

evidence.heading: The Constructive Utopia
evidence.quote: Higher levels would protect rights, ecological thresholds, interoperability, and access to appeal.

evidence.heading: The Planetary Mirror Test: Eden Before Mars
evidence.quote: The phrase before Mars is deliberately conditional.

evidence.heading: The Planetary Mirror Test: Eden Before Mars
evidence.quote: A machine that identifies local stone for autonomous construction can reuse irregular demolition material.

evidence.heading: The Planetary Mirror Test: Eden Before Mars
evidence.quote: Once construction becomes cheaper, the scarce resource migrates.

evidence.heading: The Planetary Mirror Test: Eden Before Mars
evidence.quote: The goal should not be to terraform Earth more aggressively.

evidence.heading: The Planetary Mirror Test: Eden Before Mars
evidence.quote: The paradox of the Second Garden is that better gardening in inhabited places should permit less gardening of the planet as a whole.

evidence.heading: How to Read the Quantitative Claims
evidence.quote: Every lake has a water budget. Every robot has a maintenance chain. Every beautiful place has an ecology of care.

evidence.heading: Writing as Memory and Command
evidence.quote: An archive creates institutional memory that is asymmetrical when ordinary people cannot inspect or contest it.

evidence.heading: Institutional Design Against Capture
evidence.quote: Residents must be able to challenge plans, obtain reasons, introduce alternatives, and appeal decisions to institutions that do not report to the original decision-maker.

evidence.heading: Institutional Design Against Capture
evidence.quote: Communities should be able to contract with different providers or operate critical functions locally.

evidence.heading: The Constitution of Constructive Capacity
evidence.quote: Owners and communities must be able to maintain essential machines, inspect their behavior, obtain parts, and continue safe operation when a vendor disappears.

evidence.heading: The Constitution of Constructive Capacity
evidence.quote: Planning systems should distinguish genuine ecological or safety limits from scarcity maintained for incumbent advantage.

evidence.heading: The Constitution of Constructive Capacity
evidence.quote: Rights to build create obligations to care.

evidence.heading: Epilogue: The Garden Is a Constitution, Not a Landscape
evidence.quote: Each changed the relative price of cooperation, coercion, legibility, and exit.

evidence.heading: Notes on Method and Sources
evidence.quote: The community calculations are transparent scenarios. They should not be used as engineering designs.

technicalBoundaries: Off-world capacity and local robotic construction remain conditional; no existing Mars city, imminent settlement or particular future date.
The public path and component failure are explicitly imagined examples, not empirical equipment case reports.
The stopped machine is not serviced live; no operational construction, safety bypass, excavation or repair instructions.
A finite water supply and existing wild habitat remain constraints; no numerical scenario is converted into a site-specific design.
No generic paradise genealogy, technological determinism or diagnosis of personalities.
Provider alternatives and appeal are proposed capacities, not guaranteed access, legal entitlement or environmental success.
The project remains unfinished and the wetland objection unresolved.
supersedesDefects: The prior unlabelled gate never showed the maintenance dependency described by the narration.
The historical writing line previously retained road imagery instead of showing the actual institutional record.
